line: A data Story exploring the National Postal Museum's CC0 stamp collections and the factors that makes them valuable.
insights: As a child, I loved stamps. Not having yet discovered the power of google, I would tear them off of the envelopes I found them on, and use gum to stick them onto the pages of an old diary. Obviously, that’s a terrible way to collect stamps. Slowly, as my friends and relatives started bringing me the stamps they found, I learnt of their value, their cultural and historical significance. This project aims open the world of philately to new audiences and encourage a deeper appreciation for these miniature artefacts of human history. To calculate the indices for this project, I started by identifying key factors that influence a stamp’s value, such as condition, rarity, historical context, and printing techniques. Each factor was then quantified based on specific attributes—like the presence of words such as "unused" or "mint" in the description for condition, or terms like "proof plate" for rarity. These individual indices were then weighted and combined to create a composite score that reflects both tangible and cultural aspects of a stamp’s worth. The process aimed to balance objective analysis with the inherent subjectivity of valuing artifacts, making it easier to explore the Smithsonian’s stamp collection through an accessible, data-driven lens.

line: A data story exploring the sitters of portraits in the National Portrait Gallery through the lens of gender. Portraits are grouped based on realm, and then based on the role within each realm. Portraits are further contextualised by decade.
insights: Since portraits capture the values of society at a point in time, this project aimed to explore the idea of what the sitters are remembered for. It aimed to draw focus on the proportion of the genders interested in particular realms and roles. Further, it compares the trends between men and women throughout time. All the portraits are contextualized by decade, offering insight into the ‘when’ that arises by looking at the tree maps. The audience can also explore portraits through the lens of ‘careers’, or what society at the time deemed important enough to be remembered.

line: A double page spread for a satirical piece on global warming
insights: This is an editorial infographic in the form of a double page spread. The prompt was to make an exploded view of any object. I have looked at the Earth as an object of everyday use. Hence, I have likened it’s composition to something that can be factory made, bought and sold. It is satirical, in order to bring out the humour in how lucky we are to have a place such as the Earth to live, but are still unable to take care of it. We do not treat like it is the cause of all life, but rather an object that once used, can be thrown away.

line: A dataset connecting government types, press freedom indexes, and cases of journalists who were imprisoned, killed, or went missing, enabling a deeper exploration of the relationship between press freedom and political systems. Made using Python Pandas
insights: This project focuses on creating a detailed dataset that explores the relationship between government types and press freedom by integrating multiple data sources. It consolidates information about journalists who have been imprisoned, killed, or gone missing, alongside press freedom indexes and scores such as those from Reporters Without Borders and UNESCO. Using sources like the Committee to Protect Journalists, Wikipedia (for missing journalists), and global freedom indices, the dataset highlights how different political systems—democracies, dictatorships, and other forms of governance—affect freedom of the press. The hypothesis driving this dataset is that democracies typically provide more freedom of the press, while dictatorships and conflict zones exhibit restricted press freedom, often leading to human rights violations. It examines correlations between press freedom indices and incidents of harm to journalists, exploring how government policies, war, and economic conditions impact these outcomes. The dataset aims to provide a "human-first" approach by contextualizing journalists' experiences within their countries' political and social environments. This work lays the foundation for further research into press freedom's critical role in democracy and how its erosion signals broader negative human conditions. The dataset serves as a vital tool for researchers, journalists, and advocates working to protect press freedom and human rights globally.

line: An illustrated book about having an inter-cultural identity.
insights: This book was made with the idea of identity at the forefront, and hence, character design became an important part of this process. How the character felt she was perceived at different times dictated the character’s physique, accessories, etc. This has been heavily based on the “North Indian” and “South Indian” stereotypes. The visual style was developed by scanning a page of acrylic paint, creating a photoshop brush of it, and then layering it as a stamp atop the colour and shade of the illustration.

client: Executive Office of the Secretary General, United Nations
elaborationOfClient: To better understand and prepare for complex risks, the United Nations has conducted a risk perception survey on 1,300 stakeholders across 155 countries.
tools: Datawrapper, D3.js, AI image generation, Indesign, Figma, Illustrato
line: Was the lead designer for the UN Global Risk Report 2026, which included designing the report, the banners for the event, and social media assets. The report was presented at the Singapore Mission in New York in September 2026, and its contents were spoken about in the UN General Assembly 81
insights: Political risks moved to the center. The risk of large-scale war was seen as especially prominent and increasingly imminent – 36 per cent of respondents now expect it within one year. Concerns about AI and frontier technologies, including the risk of power concentration, rose sharply. Climate change inaction remains the single most important of all 28 risks, though environmental risks as a category slightly decreased in perceived importance. Six years after the Covid-19 pandemic, attention has shifted. Perceived importance of biorisks and new pandemics fell more than any other risk measured. Joint action between governments is still perceived as the most effective response to global risks.
